writing.exampleCaption: A faster hasher is a decision about trust, not only speed.
writing.explanation:
Lookup cost depends on collisions, and collisions depend on the hash function. Rust's standard map uses randomized seeding for collision resistance, while the exact hash algorithm is not a stable public guarantee. Swapping in a faster non-cryptographic hasher is correct for internal keys and dangerous for user input.

A hash map maps keys to buckets using a hash function and resolves collisions according to its implementation. Expected lookup can be close to constant time under suitable distribution and load, but a worst-case collision pattern can degrade performance. In Rust, the standard map uses randomized seeding to make attacker-controlled collision selection harder; do not rely on one fixed hash algorithm as a permanent API guarantee. Choosing a custom faster hasher may help trusted internal keys but can weaken resistance to adversarial inputs.

The choice of key type matters too. A large string costs time to hash and compare. A small integer key is cheaper, but it may not represent the domain meaning as clearly. Hash maps do not promise a stable iteration order; do not serialize their iteration directly when output order matters. Capacity and growth affect allocation and memory overhead. A B-tree can be preferable when ordered traversal or range queries are central.

For an interview, separate algorithmic expectations from a security claim. State the key distribution, who controls keys, the required lookup rate, and whether order matters. Then explain how you would benchmark a realistic workload and test collision-sensitive behavior. The strong answer does not promise O(1) in every case or say the standard hasher is universally fastest; it connects a hasher choice to the input threat model.

Also discuss deletion: removing entries can leave internal capacity allocated, so a map that once held a million keys may retain memory after it becomes small. Rebuilding or shrinking can help when memory pressure matters. The API and version determine the exact behavior; measure the live process rather than assuming removal releases every byte.
